canonicalExplanation.summary: Before fitting any model, write a **project card** a reviewer can approve. It names the **users** and the **affected non-users** (people the decision touches who never use the tool), the **decision context**, the **task or target** and when it's predicted, where the data comes from and whether you're **allowed** to use it, a **baseline**, **metrics and slices**, key **risks**, **non-goals**, how humans **oversee** it, **acceptance thresholds** that must be met to launch, and **stop criteria** for pausing. Paired with an **experiment plan** (splits, what you'll compare, how many runs), it stops the classic mistake: building the most exciting model first and bolting on users, metrics and risks afterwards.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner starts a ticket-routing project by training a transformer, gets impressive accuracy, then discovers the model used data customers never consented to, nobody agreed what "good enough" meant, and it performs badly for one product line nobody measured. A ticket-routing card names intake-time prediction, reviewer workload baseline, urgent-miss tolerance, excluded decisions, data retention, appeal, and a stop rule for subgroup harm. In this lesson you'll produce an admin-reviewable project and experiment plan before model fitting.

sections.heading: The model: a reviewable card before any model
sections.body:
```python
card = {
    "users": "support leads", "affected_non_users": "customers whose tickets are routed",
    "task": "predict specialist-needed at intake", "data_authority": "ticket text, consented, 12-month retention",
    # What we must beat, and how we'll measure it.
    "baseline": "keyword rules; current reviewer workload",
    "metrics": ["urgent-miss rate", "reviewer workload"], "slices": ["product line", "language"],
    "non_goals": ["automatic closure", "staff evaluation"],
    # Humans, launch bar and pause rule.
    "oversight": "low-confidence tickets to humans; customers can appeal routing",
    "accept_if": "urgent-miss <= 5% in every slice, workload <= +20%",
    "stop_if": "any slice's urgent-miss > 10% for 2 weeks",
}
experiment = {"split": "time-based, last 2 months test", "compare": ["baseline", "logistic", "small transformer"], "seeds": 3}

missing = [k for k in ("affected_non_users", "data_authority", "accept_if", "stop_if") if not card.get(k)]
print("ready for review" if not missing else missing)
```


examples.title: A ticket-routing project card
examples.situation: A ticket-routing card names intake-time prediction, reviewer workload baseline, urgent-miss tolerance, excluded decisions, data retention, appeal, and a stop rule for subgroup harm.
walkthrough: **Names intake-time prediction, reviewer workload baseline:** task at intake, compared with keyword rules and current workload.
**Urgent-miss tolerance, excluded decisions, data retention, appeal:** 5% per slice, no auto-closure, 12-month retention, customer appeals.
**And a stop rule for subgroup harm:** we check any slice above 10% urgent misses for two weeks pauses the system.
examples.result: A reviewer can approve or reject the project before any model exists.

examples.title: The transformer-first project
examples.situation: A team trained a model first, then found consent problems, no agreed success bar, and an unmeasured failing product line.
walkthrough: Write the card: data authority, acceptance thresholds and slices first.
Build models only against the agreed plan.
examples.result: The project avoids unusable models and surprises at launch.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: A project plan should start with the most promising model and add users, metrics, and risks after a prototype demonstrates accuracy.
misconceptions.correction: Users, data authority, metrics, risks, acceptance and stop criteria come first; models are then judged against them.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The transformer-first project", what should have come first?

analogy.example: A project card is like **planning permission for a building**. Before laying bricks, you show who will live there, who will be affected next door, safety plans, what you won't build, and **conditions under which work stops**. Building first and asking permission later often means knocking it down.
limitations: Acceptance thresholds are the final inspection standards.
Stop criteria are the site-safety shutdown rules.
